text: This course has spent six chapters teaching you how real quantum hardware actually behaves — its physics, its honest limitations, its real benchmarks, and how to match it to a workload. This capstone asks you to put all of it into the one artifact a real stakeholder would actually read: a short, written hardware-selection brief.

A correct hardware choice that lives only in one engineer's head is barely better than no decision at all — it can't be reviewed, challenged, or revisited later. A real brief has five parts. Requirements summary: the workload's real characteristics, in vocabulary a non-specialist reader can follow. Candidate platforms considered: the realistic options, and briefly why each was in contention. The deciding tradeoff: specifically which metric separated the winner from the alternatives, and why it mattered more here. Chosen platform with honest caveats: what you're giving up and what could go wrong, stated plainly. And what would change the recommendation: the specific conditions under which you'd decide differently.

Here's a worked example. A university research group needs a small variational quantum eigensolver experiment — roughly 8 to 10 qubits, shallow per run, moderate noise tolerance, mostly local connectivity with a handful of longer-range pairs. At this scale, both superconducting and trapped-ion platforms have more than enough qubits and coherent depth — the deciding factor is connectivity versus cost. The modest SWAP overhead from those non-adjacent pairs is tolerable given the workload's noise tolerance, so the brief recommends the superconducting cloud platform, flagging that a later molecule needing many more non-local pairs would flip that call toward trapped-ion.

Notice what this brief actually draws on: Chapter 1 and 2's honest fidelity and scaling comparisons, Chapter 4's SWAP-overhead mechanics, Chapter 5's reminder that calibration drifts and numbers should be checked rather than assumed, and this chapter's discipline about metrics and benchmarks. A hardware-selection brief is where six chapters become one decision instead of six separate topics.

That's the whole course. Four physical ways to build a qubit, the control systems and calibration discipline that keeps any of them running, and — above all — the habit of asking what's actually being measured before you trust a hardware claim. Thanks for taking Quantum Hardware and Architectures.
